Appendix: A Biography of Master Xingce
Master Xingce once convened an intensive seven-day retreat and wrote this piece to instruct the assembly.
Master Xingce (1628-1682, the tenth patriarch of the Pure Land school),
at an
intensive
Buddha-
recitation
seven-day retreat he held, wrote this
instruction
for the
assembly:

In reciting the name over seven days, what is precious is single-mindedness, undivided and unpolluted; it is not necessarily the swiftness or the quantity of the recitation that counts. Only go neither too slowly nor too quickly, reciting the name closely and continuously, so that the Buddha-name within the mind is clear and distinct in every detail. Whether dressing, eating, walking, standing, resting, or lying down, let that single great name flow on unbroken and unceasing, like the rhythm of the breath itself; let it be neither scattered nor sinking away. To recite the name in this way may be called one who is able, on the level of practice, to be single-minded and diligent.
In
these seven
days,
in reciting the
Buddha-name
, what is precious is single-mindedness, undivided and unpolluted,
rather than

you need

go neither too slowly nor too quickly, reciting the name closely and continuously, so that the Buddha-name within the mind is clear and distinct in every detail. Whether dressing, eating, walking, standing, resting, or lying down, let that single great name flow on unbroken and unceasing, like the rhythm of the breath itself; be it neither scattered nor
drowsy
Reciting the
name
in this way
, you
may be
said
to be
capable,
in practice,
of single-minded diligence.
[What is meant by one who is able, on the level of practice, to be single-minded and diligent]

There are two kinds of Buddha-recitation — practical recitation and principle recitation. Practical recitation is to be mindful of Amitābha Buddha in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss; principle recitation is to contemplate one's own self-nature or to contemplate the true reality of all dharmas. Practical recitation is close to rebirth in the Pure Land; principle recitation aims at seeing one's own nature. The single mind of practice and the single mind of principle are also called the single mind, undivided, of practice and the single mind, undivided, of principle. Master Ouyi says:

“The single mind of practice is when the name is clear and distinct, free of drowsiness and distraction; the single mind of principle is when one silently accords with the Unborn and clearly understands one's own nature.”
(from the
Discussions Random Notes in the Fan Chamber,

in the Collected Works of Ouyi. [To contemplate the true reality of all dharmas] — this is true-reality Buddha-recitation. [The four kinds of Buddha-recitation] — 1. Name-recitating: calling upon the Buddha's name. 2. Image-contemplating recitation: contemplating a statue or a painting of the Buddha. 3. Visualization recitation: contemplating in accordance with the Amitayus Sutra (Contemplation Sutra). 4. True-reality recitation: contemplating the true reality of all dharmas; this true reality is the Buddha's Dharma-body, and one recites the Buddha by means of this “ultimately empty, non-existent” Dharma.)
(For more on the true reality of all dharmas, see
“The True Reality of All Dharmas”
If one is a genuine follower of the Way,
he can directly contemplate that all dharmas are thus, without a second mark — that is,
no ‘
beings and Buddhas are not two, self and other are not two, the dependent and the primary are not two, the pure and the defiled are not two, suffering and joy are not two, longing
(same as “aspiration”)
and aversion are not two, taking and rejecting are not two, bodhi and affliction are not two, birth and death and nirvana are not two.
These pairs are all of a single mark, of one spotless Way
If one is a genuine
student of the Way,
he is able directly to contemplate that all dharmas are all alike

with no difference between them. That is, beings and Buddhas are not two, self and other are not two, the dependent and the primary are not two, the pure and the defiled are not two, suffering and joy are not two, longing and aversion are not two, taking and rejecting are not two, bodhi and affliction are not two, birth and death and nirvana are not two.
All these
twosomes,
in reality
are of a single mark,
equally
pure.
[Follower of the Way] — one of the class that studies the Way.
[To directly contemplate that all dharmas are thus, without a second mark] — this is to contemplate the true reality of all dharmas, true-reality Buddha-recitation. The Buddha-store Sutra says:
“What is called the true reality of all dharmas? It is that all dharmas are ultimately empty and non-existent. To use this ‘ultimately empty, non-existent Dharma’ to be mindful of the Buddha.”
It also says:

“Seeing non-existence is called being mindful of the Buddha.” “In this Dharma, even a small thought is unobtainable; this is called being mindful of the Buddha. Sariputra, this mindfulness of the Buddha cuts off the path of words, goes beyond all thoughts, is beyond obtainable thought; this is called being mindful of the Buddha.”
(For details see
“Selected Commentary on the Buddha-store Sutra”

[All dharmas are thus] — all dharmas are alike, without difference. [Thus] means “the same.” In Buddhism, the true, unchanging nature of all dharmas is extremely hard to describe in words, so the word “thus” is borrowed to represent it. This nature is true reality, and true reality is “thus.” Because the true face of all dharmas is entirely the same, it is called “thus.”

[Dependent and primary] — the dependent retribution and the primary retribution. The lands, houses, and implements of the world, which the body relies upon, are called “the dependent retribution”; the body of a being, a false union of the five aggregates, produced by past karma, is called “the primary retribution.”
There is no need to force a contrived arrangement; simply contemplate the real as it is.
When contemplation reaches its utmost, it suddenly accords with one's own original mind.

Then one knows that dressing and eating are always samadhi; that laughter and mirth, anger and abuse are all no less than Buddha-work; and that the single-minded mind and the scattered mind are both at last but play of empty talk. Through all the twenty-four hours, one surveys
(qù)
a hair's breadth of different mark and finds it unobtainable; although one calls the name with utmost mind
(same as “call”)

, it is the same as cursing at large, and although one practices with diligent exertion, it is but bitter practice in a dream. One who understands and realizes it this way is a genuine student of the Way, single-mindedly diligent in reciting the name.
There is no
need
to force a contrived arrangement
and do anything more;
one only needs to contemplate the real as it is
: all dharmas are thus, without a second mark.
When contemplation reaches its utmost, it suddenly accords with one's own original mind
, thereby entering the single mind, undivided, of principle

. Then one knows that dressing and eating are always samadhi; that laughter and mirth, anger and abuse are all no less than Buddha-work; and that the single-minded mind and the scattered mind are both at last but play of empty talk. Through all the twenty-four hours, one surveys a hair's breadth of different mark and finds it unobtainable; although one calls the name with utmost mind, it is the same as cursing at large, and although one practices with diligent exertion, it is but bitter practice in a dream. One who understands and realizes it this way is a genuine student of the Way, single-mindedly diligent in reciting the name.
[Original mind] — the primal state of the mind. (See
“Mind, Self-Nature, and Tathagata-garbha”

The former single mind seems difficult yet is easy; the latter single mind seems easy yet is difficult. One who can attain only the former single mind is certain to be reborn (that is, he will surely be reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss). One who can additionally attain the latter single mind may ascend to the highest grade.
The
former
single
mind
undivided (single mind, undivided, of practice) seems difficult yet is easy; the latter single mind undivided (single mind, undivided, of principle) seems easy yet is difficult.
So long as you
can
attain the single mind, undivided, of practice
, you are certain to be reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss. One who additionally
attains the
single mind
undivided of principle
may ascend to the highest grade
of rebirth

Yet these two kinds of single mind are both affairs of the common mortal on this great earth; anyone who has a mind can cultivate and learn them. Monks and laity of the same hall, do not on any account set the holy state on high and contentedly remain in the lowly. Each must diligently urge on body and mind; in the near term, within these seven days, in the far term, throughout this one life, ever hold such faith, ever practice such conduct. Even if one does not attain and realize the state, the cause is still mighty, and the grade of one's rebirth in the lotus bud will surely not be in the middle or lower ranks.
Yet
these

undivided
, are both things that ordinary people can accomplish; anyone who has a mind can cultivate and learn them. Monks and laity of the same hall, do not
regard the single mind, undivided, of principle as beyond reach and unattainable
and so
contentedly remain in the lowly. Each must diligently urge on body and mind; in the near term, within
these
seven days, in the far term, through
this
one life, ever hold such faith, ever practice such conduct. Even if one does not attain and realize the state of according with one's own original mind,
the
cause
for rebirth is still most excellent
, and the grade of one's rebirth in the lotus bud
will surely
not be in the middle or lower ranks.
[Monks and laity (zi)
, su] — zi is a dark purple-black, su is white.
Monks
wear

dark purple-black robes, and lay people mostly wear white, hence the monk and laity are called “zi su.” [Affairs of the common mortal on this great earth] — affairs on the side of the common mortal on this great earth. The common mortal on the great earth (also called the common mortal of the thin earth) refers to the stage of the ordinary person. [Thin earth] — “thin” means pressed upon; the “thin earth” is the station of being pressed by all manner of suffering, referring to the realm of the ordinary person. The Pure-mind Precepts and Contemplation says:
“The foul body of the common mortal of the thin earth is lowly and mean, and its retribution is base.”

If after these seven days one turns a deaf ear, so that the familiar never grows strange and the unfamiliar never grows familiar, while ignorance and karmic habits pull and entangle one another, and one merely hopes to claim the merit of these seven days without having reached the ground of single-mindedness, then this is truly what is meant by “if one has little good roots, merit, and conditions of karma,” and how can one hope to be reborn in that land? Bringing it about that the honest words of the golden mouth are turned about and suspected of being false — whose fault is this? All of you pure ones of this seven-day assembly, I wish each one to examine himself and thereby admonish and encourage himself.
If
after these
seven days
one

turns a deaf ear to the above instruction, so that the familiar ground (meaning emotional attachment) never grows strange and the unfamiliar (meaning Buddha-recitation) remains hard to grow familiar, while ignorance and karmic habits pull and entangle one another, and one vainly relies merely on this intensive retreat's merit to be reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss, and yet during these seven days one has not reached the ground of single-mindedness — this is truly what is meant by “little good roots, merit, and conditions of karma.”
How
can one
hope to be reborn
in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss
Thus the truthful words of the Buddha's golden mouth in the Amitābha Sutra
are on the contrary suspected to be
false
; whose fault is this, after all
, then
? The pure
assembly
of this
seven-day
retreat
members,
I wish you
would each examine
and reflect,
and by this
instruction
admonish
yourselves
[The familiar never grows strange, the unfamiliar never grows familiar]
Practice means “turning the unfamiliar to familiar, and the familiar to strange.” For a recitation practitioner,
it is turning one's originally unfamiliar
Buddha-recitation
into familiar
and turning the familiar
emotional attachment
into strange

[The honest words of the golden mouth] — the Buddha instructs in the Amitābha Sutra: “If good men or good women hear of Amitābha Buddha and hold fast his name for one day, or two days, or three, or four, or five, or six, or seven days, with a single mind, undivided, then when their life comes to an end, Amitābha Buddha together with the holy assembly will appear before them. When that person dies, his mind not overturned, he will instantly be reborn in the Land of Ultimate Bliss of Amitābha Buddha.”
Master Yinguang said: “Hanshan's old vow was as yet unfulfilled, / So he appeared again, born as Jieliu
(Master Xingce)
. / He reproved those who cultivate heavenly and human blessings — / they are truly of the kind of icchantika and candala
(they are simply the likes of the icchantika and candala)

. / Buddha, mind, and my self-nature are originally not different; / The Buddha is already accomplished, I have not yet cultivated. / To gain the mind and Buddha without a hair's difference, / One must seek it in mindfulness of the Buddha and recitation of the Buddha.”
(from Collected Writings of Master Yinguang, “The Tenth Patriarch of the Qing, Xingce of Puren Monastery, Yushan”)

[Icchantika] — an abbreviation for “ecchantika” (icchantika): one who does not believe in cause and effect, commits the five heinous acts and the ten evil deeds, cuts off all good roots, and falls into the Avici hell. [Candala (zhan)] — an abbreviation for “candala”; here it refers to an evil person.
Master Xingce
, the tenth patriarch of the Pure Land school)
, a native of Yixing, Jiangsu, lay surname Jiang, style Jieliu. His father Quanchang was versed in both Confucianism and Buddhism, and had close ties with Hanshan Deqing
(he and Master Hanshan were intimate friends)
. Five years after Deqing passed away, Quanchang dreamed of him entering his room leaning on a staff, and so Xingce was born
(Quanchang dreamed that Master Hanshan, staff in hand, entered the room, and so Xingce was born)
, and for that reason named him Menghuan (Dream-Hanshan). As he grew up, his parents died in succession and he resolved to leave the world. At twenty-three he took refuge under Master Ruo
(ruò)
'an of the Li'an Monastery in Wulin, and studied under him. For five years he did not let his side touch the mat
(he sat long and never lay down to sleep)

, and suddenly penetrated the source of the Dharma. After Master Wen passed away, the Master resided at Baoen Monastery; there he met his fellow practitioner Master Ying of Xi'an, who urged him to cultivate the Pure Land karma. He also met Master Qiaoshi of Qiantang, who introduced him to the Tiantai teachings; so the two together entered a pure room and cultivated the Lotus Samadhi. His latent wisdom suddenly came through, and he fully penetrated the marrow of the teachings. In the second year of Kangxi he built a hut among the river islets of the Western Stream at Mount Fahua in Hangzhou, and devoted himself to the Pure Land karma, thus naming his dwelling the Lotus Calyx Hut
fu
, calyx)
. In the ninth year he lived at Puren Monastery on Mount Yushan, and raised up the Lotus Society; scholars gathered in harmony
(xi)
and took him as their model
(scholars unanimously praised and followed him)
Once
he wrote An Essay to Arouse True Faith, saying:
The Buddha-recitation samadhi is of long standing
(its origin is of long time past)
. Though it is said to be lofty in merit and easy to advance in, the practitioners of the last age rarely gain its spiritual efficacy — all because
(it is all because)
their faith and vow are not focused, and they are unable to guide their good practice so as to have the rebirth in the Pure Land as its aim
(failing to make rebirth in the Pure Land the essential goal)

[Guiding practice by faith and vow] — to guide practice by faith and vow, and to carry it out in practice. [Making rebirth in the Pure Land the essential goal] — for the recitation practitioner, one should make rebirth in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss the foremost concern.

Now that we have broadly invited good companions to cultivate the cause of the Pure Land, if we do not carefully examine and arouse the mind, how shall we know the essential path out of suffering? All of us who are in this assembly and attend this Dharma gathering must possess true faith. If lacking true faith, then though one recite the Buddha, keep the fasts, liberate life, and cultivate merit, one is only a good person of the world, and will be reborn in a good place to enjoy delight. When one enjoys that delight, one is thereby creating karma; and once karma is created, one must fall into suffering. Seen through right eyes, such a one is but a single step away from the icchantika and candala. Is such faith truly real?

First: one must believe that the mind, the Buddha, and beings are without difference — three are not two. I am a Buddha not yet accomplished; Amitābha is a Buddha already accomplished; the nature of awakening is not two. Though I am confused and upside down, the nature of awakening has never been lost. Though I have transmigrated through many kalpas, the nature of awakening has never stirred. Therefore it is said, “In a single thought turning back the light, one is the same as what was originally obtained.”

Second: one must believe that I am the Buddha in principle and the Buddha in name, while Amitābha is the Buddha in ultimate realization. Though the nature is not two, the stages are as far apart as heaven and abyss. If one does not single-mindedly remember that Buddha and seek rebirth in that land, one must fall into flowing transmigration according to one's karma and undergo immeasurable suffering. This is what is meant by the Dharma-body flowing through the five destinies, no longer to be called the Buddha but called a being.
[Buddha in principle, Buddha in name] — the first two of the six stages: i.e., the Buddha.

[The six stages of the Buddha] — they set forth the six positions by which a common mortal cultivates up to the attainment of Buddhahood: 1. The Buddha in principle — all beings, though they move in the six destinies and dwell all day long amid dust and toil and affliction, yet they are turned away from the body of awakening; however, the merits of Buddhahood are still fully present, hence the name “Buddha in principle.” 2. The Buddha in name — whether from a good friend or the scriptures, one hears of the Buddha-nature unborn and unperishing, inherently present in the mind, and, understanding it through the mere name, is suddenly awakened; hence the name “Buddha in name.” 3. The Buddha in contemplation-practice — not only understanding the name, one further practices contemplation in accordance with the teaching, so that the contemplative mind is clear and the principle-wisdom corresponds; hence the name “Buddha in contemplation-practice.” (The correspondence of principle and wisdom means: the principle is the sphere contemplated, and the wisdom is the wisdom that contemplates; correspondence means they match — the sphere and the wisdom are fitting and words and deeds agree.) 4. The Buddha in resemblance — at this stage, within contemplation-practice, the more one contemplates the clearer it becomes, the more one stills the more tranquil; though one has not truly awakened and realized, yet in principle one resembles it, as though one had truly realized; hence the name “Buddha in resemblance.” 5. The Buddha in partial realization — this is after the ten stages of faith, when one breaks a portion of ignorance and realizes a portion of the three virtues, thereby entering the first abiding and realizing the Dharma-body; from then on one is a great being of the Dharma-body. From the first abiding onward, each breaks ignorance and realizes the three virtues, down to equal enlightenment, going through forty-one stages and breaking forty-one portions; hence the name “Buddha in partial realization.” 6. The Buddha in ultimate realization — this is from equal enlightenment breaking the last portion of ignorance, so that delusion is exhausted and truth is pure, fully realizing the true-Thus Buddha-nature inherent in this very body, entering the stage of wonderful enlightenment and becoming a Buddha; hence the name “Buddha in ultimate realization.”
[The three virtues]
— first, the virtue of the Dharma-body
second, the virtue of prajna
third, the virtue of liberation.

Third: one must believe that though I am deep in hindrances and heavy in karma, long dwelling in the realm of suffering, I am still a being within Amitābha's mind. Though Amitābha, adorned with ten thousand virtues, is far away beyond ten million billion buddha-lands, he is still a Buddha within my mind. Since the mind and nature are not two, naturally the response and the calling meet and flow to each other, like a loadstone drawing iron — there can be no doubt of it. This is what is meant by mindful of the Buddha and reciting the Buddha, now and in the future, surely seeing the Buddha, and not far from the Buddha.
[The calling and the response meet] — the calling of beings and the response of Amitābha Buddha flow to each other.

One who possesses such true faith as above, though his good be but a hair-breadth and his merit but a mote of dust, may dedicate it all to the West and adorn the Pure Land. How much more, then, the keeping of fasts and upholding precepts, the releasing of life and the giving of alms, the reciting of the Mahayana scriptures, and the offerings to the Three Jewels — all manner of good conduct — how can these fail to fill up the provisions for the Pure Land? It is only because his point of faith is not true that he sinks into the conditioned. Hence in practicing now there is no other essential device: only add to these three kinds of true faith within the twenty-four hours, and then all the conduct
(then all the good one does)
will not have its merit cast away in vain.
Conditioned

] here refers to the conditioned cause — the karmic cause that reaps retribution in the three realms (the realm of desire, the realm of form, and the realm of formlessness). [Cast away in vain] — wasted, abandoned.
Once he convened an intensive seven-day retreat and wrote this piece to instruct the assembly:

In reciting the name over seven days, what is precious is single-mindedness, undivided and unpolluted; it is not necessarily the swiftness or the quantity of the recitation that counts. Only go neither too slowly nor too quickly, reciting the name closely and continuously, so that the Buddha-name within the mind is clear and distinct in every detail. Whether dressing, eating, walking, standing, resting, or lying down, let that single great name flow on unbroken and unceasing, like the rhythm of the breath itself; let it be neither scattered nor sinking away. To recite the name in this way may be called one who is able, on the level of practice, to be single-minded and diligent. If one is a genuine follower of the Way
(follower of the Way, one of the class that studies the Way)
, he can directly contemplate that all dharmas are thus
(“thus”, along with Dharma-nature and real limit, are all alternate names for the true reality of all dharmas)

, without a second mark. That is: beings and Buddhas are not two, self and other are not two, the dependent and the primary are not two, the pure and the defiled are not two, suffering and joy are not two, longing
(same as “aspiration”)

and aversion are not two, taking and rejecting are not two, bodhi and affliction are not two, birth and death and nirvana are not two. These pairs are all of a single mark, of one spotless Way, with no need to force a contrived arrangement
(arrangement)
; just contemplate the real as it is
(one only needs to contemplate the real as it is: all dharmas are thus, without a second mark)

. When contemplation reaches its utmost, it suddenly accords with one's own original mind. Then one knows that dressing and eating are always samadhi; that laughter and mirth, anger and abuse are all no less than Buddha-work; and that the single-minded mind and the scattered mind are both at last but play of empty talk. Through all the twenty-four hours, one surveys a hair's breadth of different mark and finds it unobtainable; although one calls the name with utmost mind
(same as “call”)

, it is the same as cursing at large, and although one practices with diligent exertion, it is but bitter practice in a dream. One who understands and realizes it this way is a genuine student of the Way, single-mindedly diligent in reciting the name.
The former single mind
(single mind, undivided, of practice)
seems difficult yet is easy; the latter single mind
(single mind, undivided, of principle)

seems easy yet is difficult. One who can attain only the former single mind is certain to be reborn. One who can additionally attain the latter single mind may ascend to the highest grade. Yet these two kinds of single mind are both affairs of the common mortal on this great earth
(they are both things ordinary people can accomplish)
, and anyone who has a mind can cultivate and learn them. Monks and laity of the same hall
(monks and laity)

, do not on any account set the holy state on high and contentedly remain in the lowly. Each must diligently urge on body and mind; in the near term, within these seven days, in the far term, throughout this one life, ever hold such faith, ever practice such conduct. Even if one does not attain and realize
(even if one has not realized and attained the state of according with one's own original mind)
, the cause is still mighty, and the grade of one's rebirth in the lotus bud
(the grade of rebirth by transformation within the lotus bud)
will surely not be in the middle or lower ranks. If after these seven days one turns a deaf ear, so that the familiar
(meaning emotional attachment)
never grows strange and the unfamiliar
(meaning Buddha-recitation)

never grows familiar, while ignorance and karmic habits pull and entangle one another, and one merely hopes to claim the merit of these seven days without having reached the ground of single-mindedness, then this is truly what is meant by “little good roots, merit, and conditions of karma”; how can one hope to be reborn in that land? Bringing it about that the honest words of the golden mouth are turned about and suspected of being false — whose fault is this? All of you pure ones of this seven-day assembly, I wish each one to examine himself and thereby admonish and encourage himself.

[Affairs of the common mortal on this great earth] — affairs on the side of the common mortal on this great earth. The common mortal on the great earth (also called the common mortal of the thin earth) refers to the stage of the ordinary person. [Thin earth] — “thin” means pressed upon; the “thin earth” is the station of being pressed by all manner of suffering, referring to the realm of the ordinary person. The Pure-mind Precepts and Contemplation says: “The foul body of the common mortal of the thin earth is lowly and mean, and its retribution is base.”

He dwelt at Puren for thirteen years, until the twenty-first year of Kangxi, on the ninth day of the seventh month, when he died at the age of fifty-five. At that time there was a certain Sun Han who fell sick and died, and revived after a full day and night. He said: “I was seized by the officials of the underworld and brought before the throne of King Yama. In the darkness I suddenly beheld a radiance that lit up the sky and fragrant flowers filling the air, and King Yama prostrated himself on the ground to welcome the Master of the Western Return. I asked who the Master was, and they said it was Jieliu
(that is, Master Xingce)
. Because the Master's light shone upon me, I was released to return.” On the same day a son of the Wu family died of illness, and revived after a night and a day
(the second night)
, and described everything he had seen, exactly as Han had done.

The eulogy says: Master Hanshan, through his former vow not yet fulfilled, returned to deliver beings, manifesting as Master Jieliu. He expanded the Pure Land, urging people to focus faith and vow to guide their practice, and to diligently recite the name, making clear the first meaning. His discrimination among Dharma-gates, and his regulations for the seven-day intensive single-minded Buddha-recitation retreat, exhaust the capacity of the Pure Land school in both understanding and practice, and fully serve as a bridge for later generations. When he returned to the West, he was revered by the underworld; the matter resembles that of Yongming
(the eminent monk of the Song, sixth patriarch of the Pure Land school)
. It may be said that the earlier patriarch and the later patriarch
kui
, measure)
are of one and the same standard
(they are indeed the same)

[First meaning] — the supreme principle, that is, neither empty nor existent, the middle-path ultimate truth of true emptiness and wonderful existence. [Discriminating among Dharma-gates] — Master Jieliu wrote an essay called “Discriminating among Dharma-gates.” [Discriminating] — also written as “selecting” or “sifting”; it means choosing. In the scriptures and treatises, “discriminating” often refers to being adept at distinguishing and selecting the right Dharma. [Bridge and crossing] — a ferry crossing and a bridge. Here it is a metaphor for the methods and path of crossing over.
